tags: 27mm adansoniadigitata africa africanbaobab afrique baobabafricain fujifilm fujifilmxt2 fujinon fujinonxf27mmf28 kenya taita–tavetacounty xt2 arbre baobab pancake plant tree végétal taita côte
description: nicolas-hoizey.photo/galleries/travels/africa/kenya/tsavo... The African Baobab is a multipurpose, drought resistant, wild fruit tree, endemic to arid and semi-arid lands of Sub-Saharan Africa. Baobab populations have been showing a lack of regeneration, and therefore causes concern for the species survival. The tree’s pulp has more protein than breast milk, more vitamin C than oranges, more magnesium than spinach, more iron than red meat and more potassium than a banana. It has become a popular additive in reinforced foods. Researchers believe baobab has the potential to become a major regional export commodity, with Southern and Eastern African regions capable of supplying 700,000 metric tonnes of baobab fruit a year.

title: Kilimanjaro - Kibo descent
tags: analogue film kilimanjaronationalpark kodachrome64 olympusom2 tanzania unescoworldheritagesite kr
description: Olympus OM2, Kodachrome 64, monochrome in Lightroom. Kilimanjaro National Park. Below Kibo's crater edge, coming out of the cloud, at around 5500m. To ascend from the Kibo Hut to the crater edge takes a normally fit and acclimatised person (not super-fit) around 5 or 6h, with a further fairly level stretch to the summit. To descend the same takes less than 2h, and on the rapid scree descent, you can feel the air getting denser, your breathing easier. The Kibo hut may be discerned in the photo. at the end of the visible path. After a break for breakfast (9 or 10h into your mountain day!) you head on further down to the Horombo Hut, which caters for both those ascending and those descending, having double the number of beds that the other huts on the route have. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Kilimanjaro fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimandjaro

title: . . . and Equatorial Ice.
tags: analogue film kilimanjaronationalpark kodachrome64 olympusom2 tanzania unescoworldheritagesite kr
description: Olympus OM2, Kodachrome 64, monochrome in Lightroom. Kilimanjaro National Park. On Kibo's crater edge, in the cloud, at around 5700m. Those who wish to experience ice near the equator in Africa don't have so very much time left to attempt the ascent . . . the article referenced below (from 2012) suggests that the ice will have gone by 2060, but more recent studies suggest sooner. The region around where I took this photo. is now ice-free. earthobservatory.nasa.gov/images/79641/kilimanjaros-shrin... www.flickr.com/photos/kimberlite/sets/72157631776444800 en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Kilimanjaro fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimandjaro

description: Olympus OM2, Olympus OM Zuiko AUTO-Zoom 75-150mm f/4.0, Kodachrome 64 Kilimanjaro National Park. The viewpoint is at around 4400m on the so-called 'Saddle' between Kibo and Mawenzi. The scree of the ascent to Gilman's point is clear, but the Kibo Hut is not in view, hidden behind the first rise. The final day's ascent from there starts at 01:00 or 02:00 and takes 6 hours or so as far as Gilman's Point, for normally fit and acclimatised people. description: Dendrosenecio kilimanjari kilimanjari Taken in the neighbourhood of the Horombo Hut at around 3700m, above the clouds. Olympus OM2, Kodachrome 64 The giant groundsels are found in the alpine zone of the mountains of equatorial East Africa . . . In the altitudes between 3400m and 4500m some of the most extreme examples of adaptations can be found, which include: Massive leaf rosettes in which leaf development occurs in a large "apical bud" Water storage in the pith of the stem Insulation of the stem by retaining withered and dead foliage Secretion and impoundment of ice-nucleating polysaccharide fluids (a natural anti-freeze) Nyctinastic leaf movement (the leaves close when it gets cold). Il entoure le Kilimandjaro, couvre une superficie de 756 km2 et est inscrit sur la liste du patrimoine mondial de l'UNESCO. title: SPOTTED EAGLE OWL 1
tags: spottedeagleowl buboafricanus kilimanjaro tanzania africa swimmingpool rescue lifesaved drowning wildlife nature wildlifephotography nigelbewley photologo appicoftheweek safari gamedrive maswagamereserve march march2019 liveanotherday
description:
Spotted eagle owl, Bubo africanus. 5 March 2019. Kilimanjaro, Tanzania, Africa.

I came across this owl in the swimming pool of a Lodge near Kilimanjaro early one morning. I fished it out with the pool keeper's net and gently put it on the side of the pool. It was very bedraggled with sodden feathers and would certainly have drowned if I hadn't rescued it. I carefully picked it up – it hissed and clicked a lot – and put it near some undergrowth where it scurried off to hopefully dry out and to live another day.

title: Akzeptiert: Der Berg ist stärker - diesmal
Kilimanjaro
tags: africa kilimanjaro trekking tanzania hiking hike unescoworldheritagesite worldheritagesite mountkilimanjaro backpacking creativecommons mountaineering day5 2007 eastafrica easternafrica machameroute canonefs1855mmf3556 400d canoneos400d kilimanjaronationalpark machamemwekaroute barafuhuts photobystignygaard
description: Barafu Huts camp, 4681m above sea level. This photo is taken the morning after a failed attempt to reach the top of Kilimanjaro. The long story: When we arrived at this camp the afternoon before, I was completely exhausted. I felt like I couldn't had crawled just a 100 meter longer (and I didn't even have energy to take at least the one obligatory photo of the camp at that time). The days walk had been the longest so far on the trek, but since I usually don't complain about a little long walk it was probably much more important that I was tired due to lack of sleep in several days. The plan was to climb the last part of the mountain starting around midnight and reach Uhuru Peak (the highest point of Kilimanjaro) around 6 o'clock in the morning to see the sunrise from the top. So after dinner we went quickly to bed to get some sleep. Almost being unable to keep myself awake while waiting for dinner, for the first time on this trek I was actually 100% sure that I was really going to get some sleep this time. And when we prepared to continue on our mission around midnight, it was the first time on the trek that I was sure that I actually had been sleeping some of the time... And after the sleep, energy wasn't really the big problem for me anymore. I had recovered quite well in the few hours. But other troubles quickly came up on our attempt to reach the top... We were four people from our team trying to reach Uhuru Peak. Jim and I plus the guide and an assisting guide. The rest of the team stayed in the camp which the plan told we would return to around noon. The night was completely dark (no moon at all) and we had only two working torches (head-torches). Apparently the assisting guide didn't feel he needed one, and the third head-light we had turned out to be broken:-/ This meant that two of us had to concentrate on following the exact foot-steeps of the person in front of us, but that wasn't really the biggest issue... I don't know how this happened, and who really is the responsible for the mistake, but we only had water in normal non-isolated bottles. And this water surprisingly quickly became frozen in the cold night:-/ Yes, I knew beforehand that we had to have water in insulated bottles on this last stage to the top, but somehow I thought it was being taken care for us besides the normal water-bottles Jim and I carried ourselves when we started the nights climb... To make things even more frustrating for me, my toes were completely frozen too after an hour of walk. I simply wasn't probably dressed for this last stage to the top. But still we continued for some time... After two hours walk Jim started to get sick in the heights, and after further half an hours walk (and guessing approx. 5100 asl.) we decided both to return to the camp. While I didn't feel any altitude sickness, the lack of water and my freezing toes made it an easy decision to turn around. We were told it was possible to get water near the top, but that was probably another three hours walk without water (and with freezing toes), so it didn't seem like an real option to continue. Also having already had a great time, i didn't think it was that important for me to actually reach the top (Today it irritates me a lot that I didn't, but that's another story:-))... But we returned back to the Barafu Huts camp to relax and get some sleep. At that time we wasn't told that the normal procedure in case of altitude sickness was to continue further down immediately, and in the morning Jim was still sick and was eager to continue further down immediately. So we then took the full descend in one long stage from here... The long descend was pretty tough to my knees and I was stupid enough to play a little football with some African boys ten days after it (Kick a ball in front of me and I will run instinctively after it like a dog after a stick...). That was probably the stupidest thing I could have done, and at the time of writing (two and half months after the descend) I still can't do any sports:-/ But hopefully that is just a matter of a little more patience before my knees are good again... Anyway, I think I have to give it another try reaching that stupid top at some other time in the future...

description:
Lava Tower Campsite (4642m above sea level) and the Lava Tower.

I got the impression that most people on the Machame Route take another path passing 112m lower than Lava Tower, but our guide apparently thought we should acclimatise to the heights as quickly as possible:-) Actually this is the highest point on our trek until the last camp before summit (which is 4681m asl.). It was a bit chill up here, and if you look closer at the picture you will see snow in the shadows. But I've seen pictures from here where everything is covered by deep snow, so we probably shouldn't complain:-)

After lunch we continued down towards tonights camp at 3985m asl...

title: Kilimanjaro
tags: africa longexposure kilimanjaro night trekking stars tanzania lowlight hiking wideangle hike unescoworldheritagesite worldheritagesite mountkilimanjaro backpacking day1 creativecommons mountaineering lighttrails startrails 2007 eastafrica canonefs1022mmf3545usm easternafrica machameroute 400d canoneos400d kilimanjaronationalpark machamemwekaroute machamehuts photobystignygaard
description: The night sky as seen from our camp at Machame Huts. I had planed to experiment a lot with long exposures of the stars in the night on the trek, having seen some amazing shots by others in the thin air in the heights. But since I didn't get any sleep this first night, and had troubles sleeping the rest of the tour, it just didn't seem right to go to bed and set the clock to wake me up half and hour later (to stop an exposure) if I actually finally did succeed falling asleep. So in the end this is the only shot I got of the stars at night. The shot is a 15 minutes exposure (the star trails are caused by the earths rotation during that period). Actually 15 minutes wasn't enough, so the shot has been "pushed" a lot in the post-processing (It is still a bit dark). If I was to do more experiments I would have had to use at least 45 min. exposures using same aperture, and probably more - I think...

title: African baobab
tags: 27mm adansoniadigitata africa africanbaobab afrique baobabafricain fujifilm fujifilmxt2 fujinon fujinonxf27mmf28 kenya taita–tavetacounty xt2 arbre baobab pancake plant tree végétal taita côte
description:
The African Baobab is a multipurpose, drought resistant, wild fruit tree, endemic to arid and semi-arid lands of Sub-Saharan Africa. Baobab populations have been showing a lack of regeneration, and therefore causes concern for the species survival.

The tree’s pulp has more protein than breast milk, more vitamin C than oranges, more magnesium than spinach, more iron than red meat and more potassium than a banana. It has become a popular additive in reinforced foods.

Researchers believe baobab has the potential to become a major regional export commodity, with Southern and Eastern African regions capable of supplying 700,000 metric tonnes of baobab fruit a year.

title: Kilimanjaro - Kibo descent
tags: analogue film kilimanjaronationalpark kodachrome64 olympusom2 tanzania unescoworldheritagesite
description: Olympus OM2, Kodachrome 64, monochrome in Lightroom. Kilimanjaro National Park. Below Kibo's crater edge, coming out of the cloud, at around 5500m. To ascend from the Kibo Hut to the crater edge takes a normally fit and acclimatised person (not super-fit) around 5 or 6h, with a further fairly level stretch to the summit. To descend the same takes less than 2h, and on the rapid scree descent, you can feel the air getting denser, your breathing easier. The Kibo hut may be discerned in the photo. at the end of the visible path. After a break for breakfast (9 or 10h into your mountain day!) you head on further down to the Horombo Hut, which caters for both those ascending and those descending, having double the number of beds that the other huts on the route have. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Kilimanjaro fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimandjaro

title: . . . and Equatorial Ice.
tags: analogue film kilimanjaronationalpark kodachrome64 olympusom2 tanzania unescoworldheritagesite
description: Olympus OM2, Kodachrome 64, monochrome in Lightroom. Kilimanjaro National Park. On Kibo's crater edge, in the cloud, at around 5700m. Those who wish to experience ice near the equator in Africa don't have so very much time left to attempt the ascent . . . the article referenced below (from 2012) suggests that the ice will have gone by 2060, but more recent studies suggest sooner. The region around where I took this photo. is now ice-free. earthobservatory.nasa.gov/images/79641/kilimanjaros-shrin... www.flickr.com/photos/kimberlite/sets/72157631776444800 en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Kilimanjaro fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimandjaro

title: . . . to Alpine Desert . . .
tags: alpinedesert analogue film kilimanjaronationalpark kodachrome64 olympusomzuikoautozoom75150mmf40 olympusom2 tanzania unescoworldheritagesite kilimanjaro
description: Olympus OM2, Olympus OM Zuiko AUTO-Zoom 75-150mm f/4.0, Kodachrome 64 Kilimanjaro National Park. The viewpoint is at around 4400m on the so-called 'Saddle' between Kibo and Mawenzi. The scree of the ascent to Gilman's point is clear, but the Kibo Hut is not in view, hidden behind the first rise. The final day's ascent from there starts at 01:00 or 02:00 and takes 6 hours or so as far as Gilman's Point, for normally fit and acclimatised people. title: Giant Senecio
tags: analogue dendroseneciokilimanjarisspkilimanjari film giantsenecio horombohut kilimanjaronationalpark kodachrome64 olympusom2 tanzania unescoworldheritagesite heathland kilimanjaro
description: Dendrosenecio kilimanjari kilimanjari Taken in the neighbourhood of the Horombo Hut at around 3700m, above the clouds. Olympus OM2, Kodachrome 64 The giant groundsels are found in the alpine zone of the mountains of equatorial East Africa . . . In the altitudes between 3400m and 4500m some of the most extreme examples of adaptations can be found, which include: Massive leaf rosettes in which leaf development occurs in a large "apical bud" Water storage in the pith of the stem Insulation of the stem by retaining withered and dead foliage Secretion and impoundment of ice-nucleating polysaccharide fluids (a natural anti-freeze) Nyctinastic leaf movement (the leaves close when it gets cold). Le parc se compose de trois sommets : à l'ouest le Shira (3 962 mètres d'altitude), à l'est le Mawenzi (5 149 mètres d'altitude) et au centre le Kibo (5 895 mètres d'altitude), le point culminant de l'Afrique.

title: SPOTTED EAGLE OWL 1

description:
Spotted eagle owl, Bubo africanus. 5 March 2019. Kilimanjaro, Tanzania, Africa.

I came across this owl in the swimming pool of a Lodge near Kilimanjaro early one morning. I fished it out with the pool keeper's net and gently put it on the side of the pool. It was very bedraggled with sodden feathers and would certainly have drowned if I hadn't rescued it. I carefully picked it up – it hissed and clicked a lot – and put it near some undergrowth where it scurried off to hopefully dry out and to live another day.

title: Red-eyed Dove nest - Streptopelia semitorquata
tags: birds tanzania ism nests columbidae streptopeliasemitorquata redeyeddove
description:
Family Columbidae- doves
This nest was in an almost leafless tree between two busy classroom buildings at ISM.  It was interesting to me that the bird chose to nest in such a hot place at the only time of year that was truly hot in Moshi.  During the day the parent was usually panting as she covered the eggs or nestlings, as shown here.  The nest failed shortly after this.  There were always Pied Crows around that surely knew about this nest.  I wouldn't be surprised if the crows considered this dove to be raising the nestlings just for the crows to eat when they got to be plump and juicy.

description: I copy how my climbing buddy commented on it from his facebook page "this is how rescues are done on Kilimanjaro. It's a 40-lb welded steel litter with a motorcycle wheel and shock absorber permanently attached. 3 people on each side. Everything is done on foot, there are no rescue helicopters in the entire country. We were lucky enough to actually see a rescue the next day, the litter attendants literally ran with the subject, over muddy and uneven ground. Amazing."

title: Jumping at the summit of the the tallest freestanding mountain on earth - 5,891m.
description: Mount Kilimanjaro is an inactive stratovolcano in north-eastern Tanzania. At 5,891.8 metres (19,330 ft) it is the tallest freestanding mountain on earth; and as the highest point in Africa, Uhuru Peak is one of the Seven Summits (The highest mountains of each of the seven continents). Due to Kilimanjaro's equatorial location and high elevation, almost every climate type on earth is represented, including a year-round snow-topped summit. While it is inactive, Kilimanjaro has fumaroles that emit gas in the crater on the main summit of Kibo. Scientists concluded in 2003 that molten magma is just 400 metres (1,310 ft) below the summit crater. Several collapses and landslides have occurred on Kibo in the past, one creating the area known as the Western Breach.There are several routes by which to climb Mt Kilimanjaro, namely, Marangu, Rongai, Lemosho, Shira, Umbwe and Machame. Of all the routes, Machame is by far the most scenic albeit steeper route up the mountain, which can be done in 6 or 7 days. The Rongai is the easiest camping route and the Marangu is also easy, but accommodation is in huts. As a result, this route tends to be very busy and ascent and descent routes are the same [Edited from Wikipedia.org]

title: Dawn from top of the Kilimanjaro - View above the clouds of the sky and stars (Uhuru Peak)
description:
This long exposure captures the start of the day as seen from the top of the Kilimanjaro. I was tired after hours of climbing and it was freezing cold. 

I had to set up the camera for the light conditions and its electronic were responding very slowly. There was delay between the time I pressed the menu buttons and when the camera actually responded to the command. I was hoping that something inside the camera didn't stop working due to the low temperatures. My thermometer-barometer wrist watch actually stopped working which was not a good sign.

The two bright spots on the bottom-left of the picture are the headlamps of other two climbers.

title: Muddy trail and dense vegetation - Montane rainforests biome
description:
Because the Kilimanjaro is located close to the equator and the Indian Ocean and because it is so high, there are five major ecological zones. Each offers flora and fauna found in few other parts of Africa. Warm moist air from off the Indian Ocean is carried to the mountain and begins to rise over the slopes. The eastern and southeastern sides of the mountain are the wettest. But as the air rises, it is sucked dry, leaving higher areas arid. The summit air is cold enough to sustain glaciers and a snowcap 

MONTANE FOREST BIOME: 
Lichens, mosses and ferns growing on trees are the most striking contrast you'll see. The most obvious is usnea, which is known as the "Old man's beard". Blue monkeys are sometimes seen.[aktrec.com]

title: Uhuru Peak
description:
Day 6.  MJP = exuberant.  SJB = cold, angry, bitter, and with a pseudo-pannus from 5 layers of clothing with Clif-bar and TP-packed pockets.

Our summit bid started at midnight, when we left Kibo Hut (15,420 ft).  The ascent to Uhuru took about 6.5-7 hours, for the measly 3.1 miles we covered.  I tried to imagine that it was like working a night shift, but that didn't work so well.  The iPod distracted me for a while, but when my playlist was over, my fingers were too frozen to select something new.

description:
Ascending Mt Kilimanjaro via Machame Route
Day 1, Leg 1
...and we're off. 4 of us in our group. I was the only one to fail to make it to the top. The first leg of the trek takes you through rainforest. You walk very very slow (pole pole), to get into the slow rhythm right from the beginning. I'm glad we walked so slow because the rainforest was just stunning. We were lucky to see some blue monkeys.

title: IMG_0551
tags: africa kilimanjaro mtkilimanjaro tanzania kili machame machameroute whiskeyroute bobbytours emmanuelmongie
description:
Ascending Mt Kilimanjaro via Machame Route
Day 2, Leg 2
Machame Hut milestone at 3000m
This is where we camped the night before at the end of our first leg. It was lovely and easy and at this point I thought there was no way I would not make it to the top because we walk so slow that even I can cope with that. Oh how I was wrong!

We had an amazing feast of a meal when we arrived, but I should have realised something was already wrong because I found it hard to eat as much as I was being asked to. I had slept barely 2 hours because our guide told me off for not drinking enough water so I drank loads at dinner time. of course this meant I was peeing every half hour all night!

The trek so far was lovely and easy, not steep at all, just a gentle climb. Next stop Shira Hut!

description:
Ascending Mt Kilimanjaro via Machame Route
Day 4/5, Leg 5 - The summit climb

The top! Well done Majid, my amazing super fit husband. This is at the end of the summit climb which is done overnight. We left Barafu Hut at 11pm the night before and started the steep and very gravelly climb. I got to a point where I couldn't even stand without feeling like I was going to faint. The blood was rushing to my head and making it throb, (though not painfully). It just felt like all the blood in my body had gone to my head. I realised I shouldn't go on so Majid and I had an emotional goodbye where the embarrassingly cheesy words "Do it for me!" were uttered. (Altitude does funy things to your mind). So we parted at about 5000m and I rapidly descended. It wasn't till I got back to the camp and puked up several times that I realised I had Majid's bag of jelly babies. He is a Type 1 diabetic, and these were the only thing that could keep him alive. So of course I panicked and couldn't sleep praying that he was OK. 

He had 7 jelly babies on him, and made it to the top with just 7 jelly babies. Unbelievable!

description:
Ascending Mt Kilimanjaro via Machame Route
Day 3, Leg 3
How anything can still grow up here is just amazing. 

When we got to the Lava Tower, I was finally sick. I had been feeling nauseous the entire morning, but found it difficult to be sick, then it finally came, at the lava tower, the point that is supposed to help us acclimatise but made me feel like hell. 

Even Majid was feeling bad at this point. He had a really bad headache and he has never suffered headaches. The French couple in our group were actually OK and there were others from other groups who were bouncing around as if they were at sea level!

There are no photos between the Lava tower and our camp because both Majid and I were feeling awful. The route to the camp from here took us through so many ups and downs I'm sure that's what made me feel even worse. I had no food in my stomach, yet it kept convulsing and forcing me to vomit what little bile I had left. 

Kilimanjaro is easy to do if you can hack the altitude. You can be a fatty who has never done any exercise in his life and make it to the top if the altitude doesn't affect you.

description: While these aren't our porters, they are the Thomson Safari porters (they all wore those bright orange suits), all porters used the same technique for carrying their loads. Note the kettle lashed to the front of the front porters load.

description: Here I am bringing up the rear of our climbing party after leaving the Mti Mkubwa camp. In front of me is in order is: Randy, Peter, Denny, Oliver, Jana, and Isaac.

title: Porter conga line.
description: We had a cooked hot lunch, served by our waiter/porter Colis, at the top of the ridge in the middle of this photo.

title: Road on the other side of valley.
description: You can see the road on the other side of the valley. This road is used for emergency evacuations and for climbers that start a Shira 1 and skip the Mti Mkubwa camp.

title: Portrait after registering at ranger hut.
description:
Every camp had these round metal ranger huts (usually 2). Every camp also had a scale--this was to weight loads and especially any trash (weight of trash was also measured at bottom of mountain to ensure that the all the trash was taken out and not dumped in the park).

This is also the place where I traded in my polartec jacket for my light weight down jacket.

title: Shira 1 camp. Approximately 11,500 feet.
description: Our tents are the blue ones to the left of the whole camp site. You can see the two round ranger huts in the middle. Behind the camp you can see the scattering of outhouses (these were of the hole-in-the-ground variety).

title: Shira 1 camp.
description: Our tents are the blue ones at the left rear of the camp.

title: Our tents.
description:
Our expedition came equipped with its own private toilet. Our toilet tent can be seen to the left of our blue tents. 

In front of the roght most blue tent you can see our dining tent (bigger olive tent) and our cooking tent (smaller beige/orange tent).

title: Porter group photo.
description:
The main purpose of this photo was to count all the paid staff so that we wouldn't be tipping phantom porters at the end of our climb. There are 21 people in this photo but we had 26 people-1 guide, 3 assistant guides, 1 cook , and 21 porters.

Guy in brown top at far left is assistant guide Adam. Sabi, our chief guide, is squatting in the middle of the photo (blue jacket plus beanie). The guy on the far right was our porta-potty porter--he carried the porta-potty everywhere on the mountain and had to clean it every morning (poor guy).

title: Shira 1 camp and Kili.
description: Early every morning and usually late in the afternoon the clouds cleared from the summit of Kili and we could see what we were going to climb.

title: Kili closeup.
description:
Uhuru peak, the summit, is just to the right of the notch on the right of the photo. The notch area is where the Western Breach tail reaches the crater rim.

On the right, lower down, you can see the lava tower. We will be passing by this on Day 4 (in two days time).

title: Morning traffic jam.
description: Porters and clients heading out to Shira 2 camp.

title: Heading to Shira Cathedral.
description: Instead of heading directly to the Shira 2 camp we headed there via the Shira Cathedral (south east of Shira 1 camp).

description: Looking to Shira 2 camp is right where the could in the middle ground is (basically right in the center of this image).

title: Kili as seen from Shira 2 camp.

description: All of us on this climb agreed that the night we spent at the Shira 2 camp was the coldest night we experienced on Mount Kilimanjaro.

title: Shira Plateau in early morning light.
Begining of challenging day number 1.
description: Today (Day 4) we will face our first challenge--climb up to the Lava tower at 15,300 feet. I felt that if I was able to make it through the day without any symptoms of altitude sickness that I was fairly confident that I would make it to the summit.

title: Lava tower rest stop number 1.
description: The trail from the Shira 2 camp to the Lava tower wasn't steep but rather a constant grade. Today would be the day that the Lemosho trail meets up with the Machame trail.

title: Twende (spelling?)
description: Twende, a Swahili word, I am told means "lets go". Here we are preparing to start walking again after taking a break. Sabi, our chief guide, is the second from the left and Adam, an assistant guide, is the fourth from the left.

title: Mt Meru in early morning light.

description:
This is the path to the Karanga camp and this section is called the "breakfast wall" because you climb this section after breakfast.

We shall be climbing this after breakfast tomorrow morning.

title: Local wildlife.
description: Hanging around to see what scraps of food can be had.

description: I am glad that I was not a porter carrying these oversized loads up the breakfast wall.

title: Karanga camp.
description:
While the camp looked close we were about 90 minutes away. The climb down into the Karanga valley was on unstable wet ground/rocks so we went very slowly.

If I remember correctly, Karanga means "peanut". Apparently one of the plants around here looks like a peanut plant. I think that I know what a peanut plant looks like but I didn't see anything around here that looked similar.

title: Kilimanjaro summit from Karanga camp.
description: The guide book warned that the Karranga camp felt like a refugee camp. We all felt that the Karranga camp was unfairly likened to a refugee camp. Now if you said that the next camp,Barfu, was like a refugee camp we would not have disagreed with you.

title: The Karanga valley.
description: You can see the path we descended on he other side of the valley.

title: Our tents at the Barfu camp.
description:
Barfu in Swahili means "ice". This camp was bad. It looked like many people went to the toilet behind the closest rock.

The plan was to sleep until dinner, at around 5pm, then sleep until 11pm. At 11pm we would get up and leave for the summit at midnight.

From the time when we got into camp and dinner we had about 2 inches  of snow. Then after dinner we got another two inches of snow along with a thunderstorm. 

When we left for the summit at midnight it was snowing horizontally because of a strong wind. It continued to snow from Barfu (15,300 feet) until we climbed above 17,000 feet.

description: The 3rd and last day before the summit of Kilimanjaro, Tanzania. Same weather each day, blue sky on the morning over a cloud sea, then the clouds rose slowly in the early afternoon till fully covering the summit. A wonderful point of view which truly deserves his nickname of "Roof of Africa", I'll never forget the sunrise at the summit after climbing all night long.
